description: Poll Tax riots, European tensions, Heseltine's challenge and Thatcher's fall in November 1990.
content_html:
The Community Charge (Poll Tax)

The policy that ultimately destroyed Margaret Thatcher’s premiership was the Community Charge — universally known as the Poll Tax. Introduced in Scotland in April 1989 and England and Wales in April 1990, it replaced the domestic rates system (which was based on property values) with a flat-rate charge per adult, regardless of income. A wealthy property owner and a low-paid worker in the same neighbourhood paid the same amount.

The policy was widely seen as profoundly unfair. On 31 March 1990, a massive demonstration in Trafalgar Square turned violent — the worst riots in central London since 1886. Cars were overturned, shops looted, and police officers injured. Approximately 339 people were arrested. The television images of burning cars in Trafalgar Square, broadcast around the world, were a severe blow to the government’s authority.

Key Fact

The Poll Tax (Community Charge) was a flat-rate local tax charging every adult the same amount regardless of income. Introduced in Scotland in 1989 and England and Wales in 1990, it provoked the Trafalgar Square riots of 31 March 1990, in which approximately 339 people were arrested — the worst civil disorder in central London since 1886.

Europe and the Cabinet Split

European policy was the other fault-line that cracked the Thatcher government. Thatcher had been a supporter of the European single market (completed in 1992) but was deeply hostile to the idea of economic and monetary union or a federal Europe. In September 1988 she delivered the Bruges Speech, explicitly opposing a European federal state: “We have not successfully rolled back the frontiers of the state in Britain only to see them reimposed at a European level.”

The speech delighted Conservative Eurosceptics but alarmed pro-European colleagues. Tensions came to a head in October 1989 when Chancellor Nigel Lawson resigned after Thatcher refused to allow him to shadow the exchange rate mechanism (ERM) of the European Monetary System. A year later, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Secretary Geoffrey Howe resigned in November 1990 over European policy, delivering a devastating resignation speech that compared Thatcher’s treatment of Cabinet colleagues to a cricket captain who “sends in his opening batsmen and then breaks their bats before they go out to the crease.” Howe’s speech directly precipitated the leadership challenge that ended Thatcher’s career.

Geoffrey Howe’s resignation speech in the Commons on 13 November 1990 is considered one of the most devastating in British parliamentary history. Howe, who had supported Thatcher loyally for over a decade, described a Cabinet in which policy disagreements were suppressed rather than debated, where colleagues were undermined in front of foreign dignitaries, and where the Prime Minister’s hostility to Europe was making British foreign policy incoherent. The speech electrified Conservative MPs who had been unsettled by the Poll Tax crisis. Within days, Michael Heseltine had announced his leadership challenge. Howe’s speech is a key example of how personal loyalty, once broken, can accelerate political collapse.

Heseltine’s Challenge and Thatcher’s Fall

Michael Heseltine had resigned from Cabinet in January 1986 over the Westland helicopter affair — a row about whether a British company should be rescued by a European or American consortium, which became a proxy battle over Cabinet government and European alignment. He had since been a visible critic of Thatcher’s leadership style within the parliamentary Conservative Party.

On 14 November 1990, Heseltine announced he would challenge Thatcher for the Conservative leadership. In the first round of voting on 20 November, Thatcher won 204 votes to Heseltine’s 152, with 16 abstentions — four votes short of the outright majority she needed to avoid a second ballot. After consulting Cabinet ministers individually and finding most believed she could not win a second round, Thatcher announced on 22 November 1990 that she would not contest the second ballot and would resign as Prime Minister.

She left Downing Street on 28 November 1990 in tears, recorded by television cameras. John Major won the ensuing leadership contest and became Prime Minister. Heseltine, ironically, did not win — he had brought down Thatcher but not replaced her.

Key Fact

Michael Heseltine challenged Thatcher for the Conservative leadership on 14 November 1990. In the first round, Thatcher won 204 votes to Heseltine’s 152 — four short of outright majority. After finding Cabinet colleagues believed she could not win a second round, Thatcher resigned on 22 November 1990. John Major succeeded her.

Thatcher’s fall was strikingly sudden, given that she had won three general elections and dominated British politics for eleven years. Several factors combined. The Poll Tax had made the Conservatives deeply unpopular in the country — polls showed Labour far ahead. Conservative MPs in marginal seats feared they would lose their seats at the next election. The European question had created a group of ministers willing to act against her. Howe’s speech had broken the political convention of loyalty and made dissent respectable. When Thatcher consulted Cabinet ministers individually on 21 November 1990, she found that each one, alone, was willing to tell her she should go — something no collective Cabinet meeting would have produced. Her leadership style — described by critics as domineering and intolerant of disagreement — meant she had accumulated enemies while the circumstances finally aligned to bring them together.
exam_tip_html: On a 12-mark ‘Evaluate an Interpretation’ question about the end of the Thatcher era, avoid arguing only that the Poll Tax caused her fall. A top-band answer agrees (Poll Tax was the immediate trigger — riots, unpopularity) but challenges by pointing to European divisions (Lawson resignation 1989, Bruges Speech 1988, Howe resignation 1990) as the deeper structural cause, and reflects on Thatcher’s leadership style as a long-term vulnerability. Reach a substantiated overall judgement on which factor was most important.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Poll Tax (Community Charge) — a flat-rate local tax regardless of income — caused the Trafalgar Square riots of 31 March 1990 and made the Conservatives deeply unpopular, creating the conditions for Thatcher’s fall.
  • European tensions divided the Cabinet: Geoffrey Howe’s devastating resignation speech (13 November 1990) gave confidence to Conservative MPs to vote against Thatcher in the leadership contest Heseltine had triggered.
  • In the first-round vote Thatcher fell four votes short of outright victory; after Cabinet colleagues advised she could not win a second round, she resigned on 22 November 1990 and John Major became Prime Minister.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Community Charge (Poll Tax) introduced in 1989-90.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any one well-described feature, for example:
• The Poll Tax was a flat-rate local tax charged per adult, regardless of income or wealth.
• It replaced the domestic rates system that had been based on property values.
[2 marks: 1 for identifying the feature, 1 for describing it]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Trafalgar Square Poll Tax riots of 31 March 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Award marks for any two well-described features, for example:
• An estimated 200,000 people demonstrated against the Poll Tax in London; the march turned violent with cars overturned and shops looted.
• Approximately 339 people were arrested — the worst civil disorder in central London since 1886.
• Television images of burning vehicles in Trafalgar Square were broadcast worldwide, severely damaging the government’s authority.
[4 marks: 2 marks per feature — 1 for identification, 1 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the end of Margaret Thatcher's premiership in November 1990.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a cause (e.g. Poll Tax unpopularity, Geoffrey Howe’s resignation speech, or European divisions) and develops the mechanism in detail — showing how the cause led directly to the leadership challenge and Thatcher’s decision to resign.
Secure: Names a clear cause with a linked explanation and some development.
Developing: Names a relevant cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without identifying a specific cause.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Thatcher's resignation for the Conservative Party.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies a consequence (e.g. John Major becoming PM and adopting a more conciliatory style, or the Conservative Party remaining divided over Europe) and develops the chain — how the consequence unfolded and what further effects it had.
Secure: Clear identification and explanation with development.
Developing: Names a consequence with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague reference without explanation.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Bruges Speech of September 1988 for British European policy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance at the time (explicitly challenged the direction of European integration, created Eurosceptic faction in Conservative Party, contributed to Cabinet resignations of Lawson and Howe) AND over time (shaped Conservative European policy for decades, fed into later Euroscepticism and debates about EU membership). Weighs extent: Thatcher remained in the EEC but set an ideological direction her successors had to navigate.
Secure: Addresses both dimensions with clear explanation.
Developing: Addresses one dimension only.
Emerging: Describes the speech without analysing significance.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The Poll Tax was the main reason for Margaret Thatcher's fall from power in 1990.' How far do you agree? Use your knowledge to support or challenge this view.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the Poll Tax (immediate trigger, riots, unpopularity) alongside deeper causes (European divisions, Cabinet tensions, leadership style, Lawson and Howe resignations). Weighs the relative importance of causes with evidence. Reaches a substantiated overall judgement on whether Poll Tax was the main cause.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence for and against the interpretation. Some weighing. Structured conclusion.
Developing: Some relevant evidence but argument is unbalanced or conclusion underdeveloped.
Emerging: Descriptive account without sustained argument.
[16 marks]

glossary_terms.definition: A flat-rate local tax introduced in Scotland in 1989 and England and Wales in 1990, replacing the rates system; universally known as the Poll Tax, it charged the same amount regardless of income.
The Poll Tax riot on 31 March 1990, involving an estimated 200,000 demonstrators; the worst civil disorder in central London since 1886, with approximately 339 arrests.
A speech by Thatcher at the College of Europe in Bruges, Belgium, in September 1988, opposing moves towards a European federal state and centralisation of power in Brussels.
Conservative Cabinet minister who resigned over the Westland affair in 1986 and challenged Thatcher for the Conservative leadership in November 1990, triggering her resignation.
Conservative Prime Minister who succeeded Thatcher in November 1990 after winning the Conservative leadership contest; known for a more pragmatic, conciliatory style.
